seo.shortDescription: Searchable 2026 U.S. tariff table for all 121 HTS Chapter 42 lines — luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks, leather jackets, belts, gloves, saddlery. Base rates up to 20% plus the extra duty by country: 10% in total for Italian and French leather goods, up to 57.5% from China.

overview.intro:
Chapter 42 covers saddlery and pet leashes, luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks and every other case or bag of heading 4202, leather apparel, gloves and belts, and articles of gut. Unlike most chapters, its **base rates are high**: 112 of the 121 tariff lines are dutiable, and the travel-goods lines of heading 4202 run **up to 20%** — 20% for plastic suitcases, 17.6% for polyester or nylon backpacks and handbags, 16% for handbags of PU or PVC sheeting, 9%–10% for leather handbags. Leather gloves pay 12.6%–14%.

The U.S. imported **$13.74B** of these goods in 2025, $11.61B of it in heading 4202. **Cambodia** ($2.22B) passed **China** ($2.21B, down 31.9%) as the largest supplier, ahead of Vietnam, Italy and France. On top of the base rate comes the **extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies — +10% for Cambodia, Indonesia, India and Pakistan, +12.5% for Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand, and **10% in total for EU goods** (nothing added where the base rate is already 10% or more). **China pays +12.5% plus +25% (List 3)** on every line except gut articles, so a Chinese plastic suitcase pays 57.5%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing extra; 14 Canadian subheadings — saddlery and dog gear, plastic and textile luggage, belts and some bags — owe a **50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA**. Exotic-leather goods also need **Fish and Wildlife Service** clearance and, for CITES species, permits.

productGroups.label: Saddlery & harness, incl. dog leashes, collars and harnesses
productGroups.blurb: Saddles, bridles and other horse tack pay 2.8%; dog leashes, collars, muzzles and harnesses 2.4% — whatever they are made of. Both lines from Canada carry the 50% Section 338 duty, even under USMCA.

productGroups.label: Luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks & other cases
productGroups.blurb: The rate follows the outer surface and the type of article. Suitcases and other luggage with a plastic or "other" outer surface pay 20%, with leather 8%; handbags of leather 9% (over $20) or 10%, of reptile leather 5.3%, of plastic sheeting (PU, PVC) 16%, of man-made fibers 17.6%, of cotton 6.3%; wallets of leather 8%; backpacks and duffels of polyester or nylon 17.6%; golf bags 4.5%.

productGroups.label: Leather apparel, gloves & belts
productGroups.blurb: Leather jackets and coats pay 6% (reptile leather 4.7%), belts 2.7%, work and dress gloves of leather 12.6%–14%, sports gloves Free to 5.5% (baseball and ice hockey gloves Free, batting gloves 3%, golf gloves 4.9%).

productGroups.label: Other leather articles (straps, belting, shoelaces)
productGroups.blurb: Leather belting for machinery 2.9%, straps and strops 1.8%, other articles of reptile leather 4.9%; shoelaces, technical leather parts and other leather articles (4205.00.80) are Free.

productGroups.label: Articles of gut, bladders & tendons (racquet strings)
productGroups.blurb: Catgut for sterile surgical sutures 3.5%, other catgut including racquet strings 3.9%, and other articles of gut, goldbeater's skin, bladders or tendons Free. Finished sterile sutures are not here (heading 3006).

workedExamples.title: Leather handbag from Italy (over $20)
workedExamples.body: The base rate is 9%. For EU goods whose base rate is under 10%, the 2026 Section 301 action charges 10% in total (9903.05.39), so a $100,000 shipment pays **$10,000** instead of $9,000. A handbag of python or crocodile leather is 4202.21.30 (5.3%), also 10% in total from the EU — but it needs CITES documents and a Fish and Wildlife Service declaration at a designated port.

workedExamples.title: Hard-shell polycarbonate suitcase from China
workedExamples.body: Trunks and suitcases with an outer surface of plastics pay 20%. China adds +12.5% (9903.05.31) and +25% because 4202.12.21 is on List 3 (9903.88.03): **57.5%**, $5,750 on a $10,000 order. The same suitcase pays 30% from Cambodia or India, 32.5% from Vietnam and 20% from the EU (its base rate is already over 10%, so nothing is added). In April–May 2025 it paid 190% from China.

workedExamples.title: Polyester backpack from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Backpacks of man-made fibers pay 17.6%. Vietnam adds +12.5% (9903.05.84): **30.1%**, $3,010 on $10,000. From China the line pays 55.1%, except backpacks that match the size description of the List 3 exclusion in U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii) (35–75 cm high, 19–34 cm wide, 5–26 cm deep), which pay 30.1% through November 9, 2026. Origin is the country where the bag is wholly assembled (19 CFR 102.21).

workedExamples.title: Leather dog collar from Canada
workedExamples.body: The base rate is 2.4%, and USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). But 4201.00.30 is on the Section 338 list in U.S. note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14), and that 50% applies even when USMCA is claimed: **$5,000** on a $10,000 shipment. A non-qualifying shipment pays 2.4% + 10% + 50% = 62.4%.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** For the purposes of this chapter, the term "leather" includes chamois (including combination chamois) leather, patent leather, patent laminated leather and metalized leather.

**Note 2.** This chapter does not cover: (a) sterile surgical catgut or similar sterile suture materials (heading 3006); (b) articles of apparel or clothing accessories (except gloves, mittens and mitts), lined with furskin or artificial fur or to which furskin or artificial fur is attached on the outside, except as mere trimming (heading 4303 or 4304); (c) made up articles of netting (heading 5608); (d) articles of chapter 64; (e) headgear or parts thereof of chapter 65; (f) whips, riding-crops or other articles of heading 6602; (g) cuff-links, bracelets or other imitation jewelry (heading 7117); (h) fittings or trimmings for harness, such as stirrups, bits, horse brasses and buckles, separately entered (generally section XV); (ij) strings, skins for drums or the like, or other parts of musical instruments (heading 9209); (k) articles of chapter 94 (for example, furniture, luminaires and lighting fittings); (l) articles of chapter 95 (for example, toys, games, sports equipment); or (m) buttons, press-fasteners, snap-fasteners, press-studs, button molds or other parts of these articles, button blanks, of heading 9606.

**Note 3.** (A) In addition to the provisions of note 2, heading 4202 does not cover: (a) bags made of sheeting of plastics, whether or not printed, with handles, not designed for prolonged use (heading 3923); (b) articles of plaiting materials (heading 4602). (B) Articles of headings 4202 and 4203 which have parts of precious metal or metal clad with precious metal, of natural or cultured pearls, of precious or semiprecious stones remain classified in those headings even if such parts constitute more than minor fittings or minor ornamentation, provided that these parts do not give the articles their essential character. If the parts give the articles their essential character, the articles are to be classified in chapter 71.

**Note 4.** For the purposes of heading 4203, the expression "articles of apparel and clothing accessories" applies, inter alia, to gloves, mittens and mitts (including those for sport or for protection), aprons and other protective clothing, braces, belts, bandoliers and wrist straps, but excluding watch straps (heading 9113).

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 42: Leather Goods, Luggage & Handbags — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 42 Tariff Updates 2026: Handbag, Luggage & Leather Goods Duties Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 42 — luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks, leather goods — since January 2025: the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (Cambodia +10%, Vietnam +12.5%, EU 10%), China List 3 and Canada Section 338, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 42 base rate changed**: all 121 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates, from Free to 20%.

Everything that changed sits on top of the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA duties reached travel goods from every country — 19% for Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand, 20% for Vietnam and 15% in total for the EU from August 7, 2025, 50% for India from August 27, and up to 145% for China in April–May 2025, on top of the 25% List 3 duty. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff**: +10% for Cambodia, Indonesia, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, +12.5% for Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand, 10% in total for the EU. China still pays the **25% List 3 duty** on 117 of the 121 lines. Since **August 22, 2026** fourteen Chapter 42 subheadings from Canada pay a **50% Section 338 duty**, even under USMCA. Duty-free programs moved too: GSP stays expired, the Nepal program expired December 31, 2025, and AGOA was renewed to December 31, 2026.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 42 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 List 3 duty and its one product exclusion, the Canada Section 338 duties, Russia's rates in lieu of column 2, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. Preference-program changes (GSP, AGOA, Nepal) are listed for reference. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a Chapter 42 product. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

No Chapter 42 line is on List 4A. The IEEPA duties on China (fentanyl and reciprocal) ended February 24, 2026, and USTR's four-year review kept List 3 in place.

inEffect.whatItMeans: Vietnamese backpacks and textile handbags pay 30.1%, plastic suitcases 32.5%, leather wallets 20.5%.

No Chapter 42 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)). The EU exception list (note 52(j)(2)) has no Chapter 42 line. This replaced the 15%-in-total IEEPA rate (9903.02.20), which ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Italian, French or Spanish leather handbags pay 10% of value — $1,000 on $10,000 — instead of 15% in late 2025 and 9% before that.

inEffect.whatItMeans: Indonesian textile handbags and backpacks pay 27.6%, leather gloves 22.6%–24%.

inEffect.exemption: Base rate + 10% (9903.05.44). No Chapter 42 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)). The IEEPA duties on India — 25% reciprocal from August 7, 2025 plus 25% from August 27, 2025 — ended in February 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Indian leather handbags pay 19%, leather belts 12.7%, leather jackets 16%, saddles 12.8%.

USMCA-qualifying goods pay no Section 301 duty (9903.05.94); others pay +10% (9903.05.55). No Chapter 42 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)). Mexico is not subject to the Canada Section 338 duties. The 25% IEEPA duty on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01) ended February 24, 2026.

No Chapter 42 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)). Three country exception lists in U.S. note 52(j) cover **every 4202 subheading**: Jordan (9903.06.20), and Guatemala (9903.06.06) and El Salvador (9903.06.09) when CAFTA-DR is claimed — so their luggage and handbags pay no Section 301 duty. Countries outside the 60 economies, such as Myanmar, pay only the base rate.

changes.title: No Chapter 42 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 121 Chapter 42 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition, and no line was added, split or renumbered.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 continues after the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the 2018 China Section 301 actions did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries because domestic industries asked for them to continue. For Chapter 42 this keeps +25% (List 3) on luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks, leather apparel, gloves, belts and saddlery.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 lists revised; Chapter 42 entries unchanged
changes.detail: Proclamations 11064 and 11065 added and removed provisions on the 9903.03.12 and 9903.03.14 lists. None of the added or removed provisions is in Chapter 42, and the September 29, 2026 Canadian import bans name no Chapter 42 product.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duty takes effect on 14 Chapter 42 subheadings
changes.detail: 50% on listed products of Canada after a 3-day suspension lapsed. Chapter 42 is on the motor-vehicle list (9903.03.14): saddlery and dog gear (4201.00.30, 4201.00.60), plastic and man-made-fiber luggage (4202.12.21, .81, .89), cotton, man-made-fiber and other travel and sports bags (4202.92.15, .31, .97), musical instrument cases (4202.92.50), 4202.99.10 and .90, unlined leather gloves (4203.29.40), belts (4203.30.00) and other leather articles (4205.00.80). Unlike the Section 301 duty, it applies to USMCA-qualifying goods too (U.S. note 51(a)).

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover all of Chapter 42
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). No Chapter 42 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)). EU goods pay 10% in total — nothing extra on lines already at 10% or more. Cambodia, Indonesia, India and Pakistan +10%; Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand +12.5%. Jordanian travel goods and CAFTA-DR travel goods from Guatemala and El Salvador are exempt (note 52(j)). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). No Chapter 42 line is on the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the base rate and the Section 301 duty on Mexican and most Canadian leather goods.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 42 subheading was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: India's extra 25% IEEPA duty removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) from February 7, 2026. The 25% reciprocal rate on India ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75) renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) makes most dutiable Chapter 42 lines Free for eligible sub-Saharan countries — including leather and plastic luggage, leather handbags and wallets, and man-made-fiber backpacks and bags — though some cotton, silk, vegetable-fiber and other textile bag lines are left out. GSP (SPI A, A*) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Nepal Preference Program (NP) expired
changes.detail: The program that let Nepal ship many travel goods, handbags and textile bags duty-free (SPI NP) ended after December 31, 2025, as the statute required. The NP code is still printed in the Special column, but no longer applies: Nepalese bags now pay the General rate. Nepal is not one of the 60 Section 301 economies.

changes.title: China List 3 exclusion for backpacks extended to November 9, 2026
changes.detail: USTR extended 178 China Section 301 product exclusions, among them backpacks of man-made fibers 35–75 cm high, 19–34 cm wide and 5–26 cm deep (4202.92.31.20, U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii), 9903.88.69), through November 9, 2026. Matching backpacks skip the 25% List 3 duty; other goods of the line pay it.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84), on top of the 25% reciprocal rate in force since August 7, 2025 (EO 14326): 50% in all on Indian leather goods, on top of the base rate. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: Cambodia, Indonesia, Pakistan, the Philippines and Thailand +19%, Vietnam and Bangladesh +20%, India +25%, Myanmar +40%, the UK +10%. EU goods with a column 1 rate under 15% paid 15% in total (9903.02.20) — so Italian leather handbags paid 15%, while EU luggage and textile bags already at 16%–20% paid no extra. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. A Chinese plastic suitcase then paid 20% + 25% (List 3) + 20% + 10% = 75% until November 9, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025, and paused the higher country rates announced on April 2 for other countries (Cambodia 49%, Vietnam 46%), which never took effect. With the 20% fentanyl duty and the 25% List 3 duty, a Chinese plastic suitcase (20% base) paid 190% until May 13, 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025, and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. No Chapter 42 product was exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, on top of the List 3 duty. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China List 3 duty raised to 25%
changes.detail: USTR raised the List 3 duty (9903.88.03) from 10% to 25%. List 3 covers every Chapter 42 subheading except the 4206 gut articles, and the rate has applied ever since.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 reaches luggage, handbags and leather goods
changes.detail: The third China Section 301 list put +10% on Chinese saddlery, travel goods, handbags, wallets, leather apparel, gloves, belts and other leather articles (headings 4201–4205).

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 42 goods were **$13.74B in 2025**, 3.8% less than the $14.29B of 2024 and well below the $17.45B peak of 2022. Heading 4202 — luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks and other cases — made up 85% of it ($11.61B); the largest single product was **other bags and cases with a plastic or textile surface (4202.92)**, $4.49B, followed by **leather handbags (4202.21)**, $2.30B.

The supplier map moved away from China. **China** fell 31.9% to $2.21B, from $3.00B in 2020. **Cambodia** grew 8.5% to $2.22B and became the largest supplier — more than double its 2020 level — and **Vietnam** ($1.70B, +11.0%), **Indonesia** ($999M, +9.7%) and **Thailand** ($423M, from $137M in 2020) kept growing. **Italy** ($1.68B) and **France** ($1.45B) supply mainly leather handbags and luxury goods. India ($775M) and Pakistan ($191M) are strongest in leather apparel and gloves (heading 4203, $1.47B in all).

Mexico ($325M) and Canada ($115M) supplied 3% of 2025 imports. The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026 and the Canada Section 338 duties from August 22); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Chapter 42 has high base rates — up to 20% on luggage and bags — and an extra duty that **depends on where the goods come from**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026: **+10% for Cambodia, Indonesia, India and Pakistan**, **+12.5% for Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand**, and **10% in total for Italy, France, Spain and the rest of the EU** — which adds nothing to EU luggage or textile bags already at 16%–20%. **China adds 37.5%** (12.5% plus the 25% List 3 duty). tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 42: Leather Goods, Luggage & Handbags — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Handbags, Luggage & Leather Goods into the U.S.: FWS/CITES Exotic Leather Rules, Marking & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 42) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 42 line needs at U.S. entry — FWS declaration and CITES permits for python, crocodile and other exotic leathers, country-of-origin marking, FTC leather labeling, CPSC rules for children's bags — and the legal ways to pay less: outer-surface classification, origin, USMCA, AGOA and CAFTA-DR, first sale, drawback, FTZ and rulings.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 42 goods need no license — but **anything made from a wild species** (python, crocodile, alligator, ostrich, stingray and other exotic leathers) is wildlife under U.S. law: it must enter through a designated port, be declared to the **Fish and Wildlife Service** on Form 3-177 and cleared before CBP releases it, and, for CITES-listed species, travel with CITES permits. Leather from cattle, sheep, goats and other domesticated animals is exempt. Every article must be **marked with its country of origin**, and the FTC Leather Guides govern what may be called "leather".

On cost, base rates of up to 20% and an extra duty by country leave real room: the **outer surface** decides the rate (a leather handbag pays 9%, a PU one 16%, a polyester one 17.6%), the **country of origin** decides the extra duty (+10% Cambodia, +37.5% China), and USMCA, AGOA, CAFTA-DR, first-sale valuation, drawback and foreign-trade zones lower the bill further. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Classify by the outer surface — and the value break on leather handbags
levers.saves: The gap between outer-surface rates: a handbag pays 9%–10% in leather, 16% in plastic sheeting (PU, PVC), 17.6% in polyester or nylon and 6.3% in cotton; luggage pays 8% in leather and 20% in plastics
levers.appliesTo: Heading 4202 — luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks and cases
levers.document: Product specifications showing the material that makes up the exterior surface, including how coated or laminated fabrics are built.
levers.caveat: The outer surface is what the classification follows; a coated textile counts as textile or plastic depending on which makes up the exterior (additional U.S. note 2). Leather handbags valued not over $20 pay 10%, over $20 9%. Design and material are commercial choices — the declared classification must match the goods, and a ruling settles doubtful cases.

levers.title: Know the country of origin — and where a bag gets it
levers.saves: The difference between country rates: +10% for Cambodia or India, +12.5% for Vietnam, 10% in total for the EU, +37.5% for China
levers.appliesTo: All lines; the gap is widest on luggage and bags from China
levers.document: Production records showing where the article was made: for textile bags (4202.12.40–.89, 4202.22.40–.89, 4202.32.40–.99, 4202.92.04–.08, .15–.33, .60–.97) where it was wholly assembled; for leather and other bags, where it was last substantially transformed.
levers.caveat: Cutting in one country and sewing in another, or only adding trim, labels or packaging, may not move the origin. The Section 301 and 338 duties follow the country of origin, and CBP can ask for proof.

levers.document: The origin proof each program requires (a certification or declaration of origin, or the AGOA/CBTPA documentation) and records to back it up.
levers.caveat: An FTA removes the base rate but, except where a note 52(j) list says otherwise, not the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)). AGOA (D) runs to December 31, 2026 and leaves out some cotton, silk, vegetable-fiber and other textile bag lines. GSP (A, A*) has been expired since December 31, 2020 and the Nepal program (NP) since December 31, 2025, although both codes are still printed.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a), (j)

levers.title: Use the China List 3 exclusion for qualifying backpacks
levers.saves: The 25% List 3 duty on Chinese backpacks of man-made fibers that match the exclusion description
levers.appliesTo: 4202.92.31.20 — backpacks with an outer surface of man-made fibers, 35–75 cm high, 19–34 cm wide and 5–26 cm deep
levers.document: Product dimensions and materials showing the backpack matches the description; report 9903.88.69 instead of 9903.88.03.
levers.caveat: In effect through November 9, 2026 unless USTR extends it again. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.31) still applies.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii), 9903.88.69

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Every ad valorem duty is charged on a lower value — the base rate and the 10%–50% extra duties included — when the factory price to a trading company or brand owner is lower than the price you pay
levers.appliesTo: All lines bought through a trading company, agent-buyer or brand owner rather than straight from the maker
levers.document: Proof that the first sale was a bona fide sale for export to the United States at arm's length: the factory invoice, contracts and payment records.
levers.caveat: Only a sale clearly destined for the U.S. qualifies, and the importer must be able to show the earlier price at entry.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export or destroy
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported goods (or goods made from them) are exported or destroyed
levers.appliesTo: Any line — for example handbags or luggage re-exported to Canadian or Latin American stores
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import, manufacturing and export records.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Hold, kit or relabel goods in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: No duty on goods re-exported from the zone, and duty deferred until goods leave it for the U.S. market
levers.appliesTo: Any line — useful for luggage and handbags distributed to several countries
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's inventory records.
levers.caveat: Goods entered for U.S. consumption from a zone pay the duties in force on the entry date; wildlife rules still apply.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision for U.S. goods coming back
levers.saves: All duty on U.S.-made goods returned unchanged (9801.00.10), for example unsold stock sent back by a foreign distributor
levers.appliesTo: Any line, for American goods returned without having been advanced in value or improved abroad
levers.document: Proof of U.S. origin and of the export, as CBP requires for the provision.
levers.caveat: The Section 301 and 338 duties also do not apply to goods properly entered under Chapter 98, except subchapter XXIII and 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 (U.S. notes 51(a) and 52(a)).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51(a), 52(a)

levers.title: Get a binding classification ruling
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate and the extra duty: handbag (4202.2x) versus pocket article (4202.3x) or travel bag (4202.92); coated fabric counted as textile or plastic; a bag on or off the Canada Section 338 list
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the material, construction or use decides the line
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the article, its outer surface, dimensions and use.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a changed design or material may need a new one.

rules.title: Wildlife products — exotic leathers such as python, crocodile, alligator, lizard, ostrich or stingray — must enter at a designated port, be declared on Form 3-177 and be cleared by FWS before CBP releases them. Domesticated animals (cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and others listed in 50 CFR 14.4) are exempt
A business importing wildlife products for sale needs an FWS import/export license

Products of CITES-listed species need the CITES documents for their appendix — an export permit or re-export certificate, and an import permit for Appendix I species; crocodilian skins and products follow added tagging and labeling rules, and American alligator products have their own rules

Country-of-origin marking in English, legible, indelible and permanent enough to reach the ultimate purchaser — on the bag, wallet, belt or glove itself or its retail container; a U.S. place name on the article requires the origin marking near it
Textile travel goods and bags (4202.12.40–.89, 4202.22.40–.89, 4202.32.40–.99, 4202.92.04–.08, .15–.33, .60–.97) are "textile products": their origin is the country where they were wholly assembled

Leather Guides: luggage, handbags, wallets, belts and similar articles may not be called "leather" unless made in all substantial parts of leather; imitation, bonded, split or embossed leather must be disclosed

Backpacks, bags and cases designed or intended primarily for children 12 or younger are children's products: lead limits for paint and coatings, third-party testing and a Children's Product Certificate
Catgut imported to make sterile surgical sutures (4206.00.13): the finished absorbable gut suture is an FDA-regulated medical device

Report the Chapter 99 headings with the line: the 2026 Section 301 heading for the country (or its note 52(j) exemption), China List 3 (9903.88.03) or its exclusion (9903.88.69), Brazil (9903.05.01), Canada Section 338 (9903.03.14)

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 30, 50–52

groups.label: Saddlery & harness, incl. dog leashes, collars and harnesses
groups.note: No agency license for saddlery or dog gear of cattle leather, textiles or plastics. Both lines from Canada pay the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

groups.label: Luggage, handbags, wallets, backpacks & other cases
groups.note: Bags of exotic leather (reptile lines 4202.21.30 and 4202.31.30, and any leather from a wild species) need FWS clearance and, for CITES species, permits. Textile bags take their origin from where they are wholly assembled. The outer surface decides the line and rate: 8%–10% for leather, 16%–20% for plastics, 17.6% for man-made fibers.

groups.label: Leather apparel, gloves & belts
groups.note: Reptile-leather apparel and accessories (4203.10.20, 4203.40.30) are wildlife products. Leather gloves carry the chapter's other high rates (12.6%–14%); 4203.29.40 gloves and 4203.30.00 belts from Canada pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Other leather articles (straps, belting, shoelaces)
groups.note: Reptile-leather articles (4205.00.60) are wildlife products. 4205.00.80 from Canada pays the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Articles of gut, bladders & tendons (racquet strings)
groups.note: Sterile surgical catgut is not here (heading 3006). Gut articles are on no China Section 301 list, so Chinese goods pay only the 12.5% 2026 duty.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs and import rules for handbags, luggage, backpacks, wallets and other leather goods. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: 112 of the 121 Chapter 42 lines carry a base duty, and travel goods are among the highest-rated consumer goods: 20% for plastic luggage, 17.6% for polyester or nylon bags and backpacks, 16% for PU handbags, 9%–10% for leather handbags.

Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty is added by country: +10% for Cambodia, Indonesia, India and Pakistan, +12.5% for Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand, and 10% in total for the EU — nothing extra on EU goods already at 10% or more.
China pays the most: +12.5% plus +25% (List 3) on every line except gut articles — 57.5% on plastic suitcases, 55.1% on polyester backpacks.

USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing. From Canada, 14 subheadings — saddlery and dog gear, plastic and textile luggage, some travel bags, belts — pay a 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

The IEEPA duties (up to 190% on Chinese luggage in spring 2025, 19%–20% on Cambodia and Vietnam from August 2025) ended February 24, 2026; the 10% Section 122 surcharge ended July 23, 2026. GSP and the Nepal program have expired; AGOA runs to December 31, 2026.
Exotic leathers (python, crocodile, ostrich) need Fish and Wildlife Service clearance and, for CITES species, permits; every article must be marked with its country of origin.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on handbags imported into the U.S.?
faqs.answer: Yes. The base rate depends on the outer surface: leather handbags pay 9% (over $20) or 10%, reptile leather 5.3%, plastic sheeting such as PU or PVC 16%, man-made fibers 17.6%, cotton 6.3%. Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty is added by country: Italy, France and the rest of the EU 10% in total, Japan 12.5% in total (so a Japanese leather handbag pays 12.5%), Cambodia and India +10%, Vietnam +12.5%, China +37.5%. USMCA-qualifying handbags from Mexico or Canada pay nothing.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on luxury and designer bags from Italy and France?
faqs.answer: A leather handbag, wallet or belt from Italy or France pays 10% of its customs value in total since July 24, 2026 (9903.05.39) — $500 on a $5,000 bag — instead of 15% between August 2025 and February 24, 2026 and 9% before 2025. Bags with a base rate of 10% or more, such as nylon or PU handbags and textile or plastic luggage, pay only that base rate. Italy supplied $1.68B and France $1.45B of Chapter 42 goods in 2025. A bag of python or crocodile also needs CITES documents and an FWS declaration.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on handbags and leather goods from China?
searchedAs: tariffs on leather goods from china
import duty on bags from china
faqs.answer: Chinese Chapter 42 goods pay the base rate plus 12.5% (2026 Section 301, 9903.05.31) plus 25% (List 3, 9903.88.03): 46.5% on a leather handbag over $20, 53.5% on a PU handbag, 55.1% on a polyester backpack or handbag, 45.5% on a leather wallet, 40.2% on a leather belt. Backpacks matching the size description of the note 20(vvv)(iii) exclusion skip the 25% through November 9, 2026. China supplied $2.21B in 2025, 31.9% less than in 2024.

faqs.question: What is the import duty on luggage and suitcases?
searchedAs: import duty on luggage from china
faqs.answer: Suitcases and trunks with an outer surface of plastics (hard-shell luggage) pay 20%, of man-made fibers 17.6%, of leather 8%. Add the extra duty by country: 57.5% in total for a Chinese hard-shell suitcase, 30% from Cambodia, India or Indonesia, 32.5% from Vietnam or Thailand, 20% from the EU (nothing is added at 10% or more). Plastic and man-made-fiber luggage from Canada also pays 50% Section 338, even under USMCA.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on leather goods from India to the USA?
searchedAs: tariff on leather goods from india to usa
tariff on leather goods from india
faqs.answer: Base rate plus 10% Section 301 (9903.05.44) since July 24, 2026: 19% for a leather handbag over $20, 16% for a leather jacket, 12.7% for a belt, 12.8% for a saddle, 22.6%–24% for leather gloves. The IEEPA duties on India — 50% from August 27, 2025 — ended in February 2026. India supplied $775M of Chapter 42 goods in 2025.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on bags and luggage from Cambodia?
faqs.answer: Since July 24, 2026 Cambodian goods pay the base rate plus 10% Section 301 (9903.05.28): 27.6% for a polyester backpack or handbag, 30% for a plastic suitcase, 19% for a leather handbag. The 19% IEEPA reciprocal tariff (from August 7, 2025) ended February 24, 2026, and the 49% rate announced in April 2025 never took effect. Cambodia was the largest Chapter 42 supplier in 2025 ($2.22B).

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on bags and luggage from Vietnam?
faqs.answer: Base rate plus 12.5% Section 301 (9903.05.84) since July 24, 2026: 30.1% for a polyester backpack or handbag, 32.5% for a plastic suitcase, 20.5% for a leather wallet. The 20% IEEPA reciprocal tariff (August 7, 2025 to February 24, 2026) has ended. Vietnam supplied $1.70B of Chapter 42 goods in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for handbags and purses?
searchedAs: hs code for handbags of leather
faqs.answer: Handbags are 4202.21 (outer surface of leather), 4202.22 (plastic sheeting or textile) and 4202.29 (other). In the U.S. schedule: leather handbags 4202.21.60.00 (valued not over $20, 10%) or 4202.21.90.00 (over $20, 9%), reptile leather 4202.21.30.00 (5.3%), PU or PVC 4202.22.15.00 (16%), polyester or nylon 4202.22.81.00 (17.6%), cotton 4202.22.45.00 (6.3%). Small purses and wallets carried in a handbag are 4202.31 or 4202.32; tote bags are classed as handbags or shopping bags by design and surface.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for luggage and suitcases?
faqs.answer: Suitcases, trunks and similar containers are 4202.11 (leather, 4202.11.00, 8%), 4202.12 (plastics: 4202.12.21, 20%; man-made fibers: 4202.12.81, 17.6%) and 4202.19 (other, 20%). Hard-shell suitcases use 4202.12.21.20 ("structured, rigid on all sides"). Duffel and other travel bags are 4202.91 (leather, 4.5%) or 4202.92 (textile or plastic, mostly 17.6%–20%).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a backpack or laptop bag?
faqs.answer: Backpacks are travel, sports and similar bags of 4202.92 (additional U.S. note 1): polyester or nylon backpacks are 4202.92.31.20 (17.6%), cotton 4202.92.15.00 (6.3%). A laptop case shaped like a briefcase is usually an attache or briefcase-type container of 4202.11 or 4202.12 (4202.12.81.30 in man-made fibers, 17.6%). Backpacks for children 12 and under also need a CPSC Children's Product Certificate.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a wallet?
faqs.answer: Wallets, card cases and coin purses are articles carried in the pocket or handbag: leather 4202.31.60.00 (8%), reptile leather 4202.31.30.00 (3.7%), plastic sheeting 4202.32.20.00 (20%) or 4202.32.10.00 (reinforced or laminated plastics, 12.1¢/kg + 4.6%), man-made fibers 4202.32.93.00 (17.6%).

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for leather belts, gloves and jackets?
searchedAs: hs code for leather golf gloves
faqs.answer: Leather belts are 4203.30.00.00 (2.7%), leather jackets and coats 4203.10.40 (6%; reptile leather 4203.10.20, 4.7%), leather work and dress gloves 4203.29 (12.6%–14%), golf gloves 4203.21.80.30 (4.9%), batting gloves 4203.21.20 (3%). Fur-lined leather apparel is in Chapter 43 and leather watch straps in heading 9113. Belts and unlined 4203.29.40 gloves from Canada pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for dog leashes, collars and saddles?
faqs.answer: Dog leashes, collars, muzzles and harnesses of any material are 4201.00.30.00 (2.4%); saddles, bridles and other saddlery and harness for any animal 4201.00.60.00 (2.8%). Stirrups, bits and buckles entered separately are not here (Chapter 42, note 2(h)). From China both lines pay 37.5% extra; from Canada 50% Section 338, even under USMCA.
